colorfle-answer-today.articleHtml:
Colorfle challenges you to identify three RGB source colors that blend into a given target through additive mixing. Unlike paint pigments, light colors add together—so red plus green reads as yellow, green plus blue becomes cyan, and all three primaries together produce white. What the source colors are telling you

The clue widgets on this page break down the target's hue, saturation, and brightness separately. A careful player notices that each component maps directly to one of your three guesses. If the target skews warm, one of your sources needs strong red values. Cool undertones demand blue-heavy inputs. The hint system narrows which channel is off when you're close but not exact.

Randomly cycling through combinations wastes moves. Additive color math lets you reverse-engineer the solution. Each RGB channel ranges from 0 to 255—split the target's channel value by three and assign roughly equal portions to your three sources. For example, if the target shows R:180, G:90, B:45, each source might contribute R-values around 60, G-values around 30, and B-values around 15. Refine from there based on the reveal feedback.

The Colorfle archive shows patterns across recent puzzles. Targets with high saturation tend to require bold primary-adjacent colors rather than muted pastels. Low-brightness targets often hide near-black solutions where one dominant channel carries most of the weight.

Does the order of my three color selections matter?

No. Additive mixing is commutative—the result stays the same regardless of sequence. What matters is hitting the correct combined values across all three inputs.

Additive mixing combines light (RGB). Subtractive mixing applies to pigments like paint or ink (CMYK). Colorfle operates on light physics, so combining red and green produces yellow, not brown.

Yes. You can enter identical values across all three slots if the math supports it. This sometimes happens with very dark or very light targets where one dominant channel drives the result.

Neutral targets require balanced RGB contributions across all three sources. Aim for roughly equal values in each channel—something like R:85, G:85, B:85 distributed across your guesses. Avoid pushing any single channel too high or you'll shift the target's hue.

Mix those up and you'll end up searching the wrong hemisphere entirely. The hint widget shows both values clearly—take two seconds to confirm which number is which before you start scanning maps.

It means words that appear in similar contexts across training data tend to score higher together. "Coffee" and "morning" score well because they co-occur frequently. "Coffee" and "geology" score poorly despite both being nouns. The model learned associations, not definitions.
